patient.chief_complaint: Sudden severe headache and chest pain simultaneously - concerned about heart attack
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Lewis is a 58-year-old man with CAD on dual antiplatelet therapy who presents with simultaneous sudden onset severe headache and chest pain. He was lifting boxes at home when he experienced sudden onset of what he describes as 'the most horrible headache and chest pain at the same time.' The headache reached 10/10 within seconds. Chest pain was pressure-like, substernal, 7/10. He called 911. EMS found BP 218/128 mmHg. He was given aspirin 325 mg additional dose by EMS and was rushed to the ED for concern of STEMI. ECG in the field showed deep T-wave inversions V1-V4 leading to cardiac catheterization consideration. He is on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for a stent placed 2 years ago. The primary team is focused on the cardiac presentation. The neurology consult was triggered by the ER nurse who noted the headache was described as 'thunderclap' and he has neck stiffness. The diagnostic challenge: 1) STEMI vs. neurogenic cardiac changes from SAH; 2) dual antiplatelet therapy complicates SAH management and intervention; 3) the cardiac and neurological presentations are simultaneously present.

interactions: Aspirin + clopidogrel combination: irreversibly inhibits platelet aggregation - increased surgical/procedural bleeding risk in SAH
contraindications: Continue dual antiplatelet in setting of SAH with planned endovascular coiling = increased procedural hemorrhage risk
warnings: CRITICAL: Patient on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) with confirmed SAH and aneurysm requiring treatment

Risk of stent thrombosis in coronary stent if clopidogrel stopped: stent placed 2 years ago - risk of thrombosis lower than within first year
Cardiology must be involved in decision to hold clopidogrel

alternatives: Consider bridging with GpIIb/IIIa inhibitor for coronary stent while holding oral antiplatelets - discuss with cardiology

output.query: SAH neurogenic T-wave inversion STEMI differentiation Takotsubo troponin elevation

results.finding: Deep symmetric T-wave inversions without ST elevation in SAH = neurogenic ECG, not STEMI
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy occurs in 20-30% of SAH - elevated troponin and wall motion abnormalities
Echocardiogram is the key test to distinguish neurogenic Takotsubo (apical ballooning) from STEMI (regional wall motion by coronary territory)
Catheterization rarely changes SAH management acutely; delays neurosurgical treatment

output.summary: Neurogenic cardiac manifestations including ECG abnormalities and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy occur in a substantial proportion of patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Echocardiography distinguishes Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis) from regional wall motion abnormalities in a coronary distribution. Troponin elevation in the setting of acute neurological injury does not reliably indicate acute coronary syndrome. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Mild bilateral anterior circulation hypoperfusion without established infarction. Preserved cerebral blood volume bilaterally. Mildly prolonged time-to-peak in the bilateral ACA/MCA territories. Findings are consistent with early vasospasm without completed infarction. Clinical correlation recommended.

key_reasoning_points: Simultaneous thunderclap headache + chest pain/ECG changes = SAH until proven otherwise; CT head before cardiac cath
Deep SYMMETRIC T-wave inversions without ST elevation in SAH are neurogenic - classic Wellens-like pattern but from catecholamine surge
Echocardiogram: Takotsubo shows apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis; STEMI shows regional hypokinesis in coronary territory
Dual antiplatelet therapy complicates SAH management: must hold before intervention; coordinate with cardiology re: stent thrombosis risk (2-year-old stent has lower risk)
Troponin 2.8 ng/mL is from Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, not plaque rupture - cardiac catheterization would show minimal or no disease
SAH as primary event causing neurogenic cardiac injury vs primary cardiac event with coincidental headache - CT confirms SAH as primary
